SLOs: The course will help you develop strategies to read the complex texts demanded of you in college, texts that contain sophisticated vocabulary, nuanced ideas and expectations of background information. We will also look very closely at how writing is planned, executed and revised—examining draft writing to determine how to improve it (in terms of ideas, writing style and editing (spelling, punctuation, grammar). This course allows for individual attention to your specific literacy challenges.The goal is for you to successfully complete the assignments in English 401. At the same time, you will take away from this class several strategies that you can tailor to your next challenges in reading, writing, thinking and researching.

SLOs:
Mobile computing is ubiquitous and fast growing. In 2011 there were 6 billion mobile subscriptions, 1.2 billion mobile Web users, and 1.78 billion mobile devices world-wide. International Data Corporation predicts that global downloads of mobile apps will reach 76.9 billion in 2014 and will be worth $35 billions.

The course introduces mobile computing and teaches computational thinking – a fundamental problem-solving skill for everyone, not only for computing professionals. In a larger picture, computational thinking is a problem-solving process that makes extensive use of computing concepts and strategies.

Computational thinking skills are built by exercising seven big ideas: creativity, abstraction, data analysis, algorithms, programming, digital devices and the Internet, and impacts of computing within economic, social, and cultural contexts.

The course seeks to broaden participation in computing by attracting students from communities with long-standing underrepresentation in computing: women, persons with disabilities, underrepresented students of color, and underserved students, such as low-income and first generation students.
